topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Digit Emergence
target_audience: University students with a background in basic mechanics

sections.title: The Hook: An Impossible Connection
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: how the collision of two blocks with mass ratios of powers of 100 calculates the digits of pi. Establish the surprise factor.
sections.example: Imagine two blocks, one massive (mass M) and one tiny (mass m=1), sliding toward each other. The number of total collisions equals the digits of pi.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review the conservation of momentum and kinetic energy in perfectly elastic collisions. Introduce the 'V-Space' coordinate system as a geometric representation.
sections.example: Using a 2D velocity graph: represent the velocity of block A on the x-axis and block B on the y-axis. A collision is a reflection across a line defined by the mass ratio.

sections.title: Geometric Mapping: From Collisions to Arcs
sections.content: Explain how the velocity vectors transition from a linear trajectory to an elliptical arc in phase space. The scaling factor of the mass (100^n) creates the specific curvature of a circle.
sections.example: Visualize the velocity state as a point moving on an ellipse. When the mass ratio is 100^n, the ellipse becomes a circle, and the number of 'bounces' represents the arc length or pi.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Demonstration: The 1-100 Case
sections.content: Walk through the visualization: Block A hits Block B, which hits the wall, which hits Block A. Show how the geometry of the collision cycle maps to pi ≈ 3.14.
sections.example: An animation of a large block (100kg) and a small block (1kg) colliding. Counting the bounces: 3, then 1, then 4—the first three digits of pi emerge mathematically.

sections.title: Synthesis & Summary
sections.content: Summarize that this is not a 'magic trick' but a consequence of the conservation laws and the geometric interpretation of elastic collisions. Conclude with the beauty of mathematics in physical systems.
sections.example: Final slide showing a 'Mechanical Computer' calculating pi, connecting the abstract constant of a circle to the physical momentum of moving objects.
